html:
The map's label for the foraging peoples of the tropical grasslands of South America, shown from 1500 BCE to 1715. The great savannas are the Llanos of the Orinoco basin, in what is now Venezuela and Colombia, and the cerrado of central Brazil. The label is broad and covers many peoples whose past is known mostly from archaeology and from accounts written after 1500.

The savannas have a long dry season and a wet season that floods the lowlands. People there:

  • hunted deer, rhea, armadillo and peccary, often with fire to drive game;
  • fished in rivers and lagoons as they shrank in the dry season;
  • gathered palm fruit, nuts, roots and honey;
  • often grew some crops at forest edges, so the line between foragers and manioc farmers was blurred.

In central Brazil, peoples of the Jê language family later became known for large circular villages. To the north and west lay the forests of the Amazon peoples, and along the Atlantic coast the Tupi.

After 1500 the savannas changed fast. Cattle and horses from Europe, part of the Columbian Exchange, spread over the Llanos under Spanish rule, and Jesuit missions gathered people into towns. In Brazil, slave raiders from São Paulo pushed inland through the 1600s in search of captives and gold, and the Portuguese colony slowly took over the cerrado.
